## The founder-emulation items

1. **Who (practitioner `agent`).** YC-C names hotel groups with "call centers and central reservation departments";
   YC-L's video features front-desk staff at a Munich hotel. *My choice:* the reservation agent, central office or
   front desk, who sees the missed-call list. Segment: hotel groups in Germany with a central office or call center.
2. **When (circumstance, occasion, window).** YC-L's "After hours. During peak hours. On holidays." *My choice:* the
   occasion "reservation shift", window the last 7 days (calls come in on every shift; spec 120's "every shift" -> 7
   DAYS), Frequency 5 to 7 days out of 7.
3. **Who pays (decision-maker `director`, Buyer and payer, Purchase friction).** TERMS addresses the hotel group;
   YC-L asks to "book a 10-minute call if you lead a hotel group". *My choice:* the revenue or reservations director
   decides, the hotel's owner has to agree. Purchase friction tests "A data protection review of guest calls" (German
   hotels handle guests' card and personal data on the call); my choice, no source names it.
4. **Mechanism.** YC-C: missed calls forwarded to Codyco, the AI answers, bookings appear in the PMS. Compatibility
   tests call forwarding (the mechanism needs it); Adoption friction tests letting the AI answer in the hotel's voice.
5. **Cost, price, ability.** As in the table. Reading `budget` by the engine (a percent of calls against euros).
6. **Commitment.** TERMS and YC-L: the paid, money-back pilot at one location. The step carries its number ("pay
   €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel"), the gap-8 check.

## The respondents

No first-person account by a German reservation agent or revenue director was found in public (no HN thread; the
site's quotes are curated testimonials). **Every person is the author's invention**, no real person's name is used,
and each is built on the public facts named here.

Reservation agents (Parts 1 and 2):
- Lena Hoffmann: a trade-fair Saturday in a Munich central office; built on YC-L ("During peak hours") and the Munich
  hotel YC-L features.
- Murat Yilmaz: a check-in rush at the desk; YC-L's "peak hours".
- Chiara Russo: a group whose call center already answers after hours (YC-C: "Even with call centers..."); her pain is
  group emails, so Importance and Current solution go against the founder.
- Jonas Weber: alone on a Sunday desk; YC-L's "On holidays" / after hours.
- Aylin Demir: an old phone system that cannot forward (Compatibility only_with_help); the author's.
- Tobias Brandl: the sceptic who will not hand guests to an AI (Relative advantage negative, Adoption no); the author's.
- Elif Kaya: weekend abandoned calls seen on Monday; YC-L's "After hours".
- Daniel Okonkwo: rates pushed wrong to agencies matter more (Importance against); the author's.
- Mehmet Arslan: a vague story, GUESSED. Katarina Novak: a story chip, GUESSED.
- Florian Gruber, Nadia Haddad: gate No (no unanswered booking call in the 7 days).

Revenue directors (COMMERCIAL_B2B link, Part 3): Stefanie Wagner (6%), Andreas Keller (4%, below the founder's 5%),
Roberto Bianchi (8%), Ingrid Lindholm (2%, a call center covers after hours), Karim Benali (does not know his rate;
YC-L's "Free AI Strategy Workshop" and SITE's free test number as his ask), Petra Vogel (5%), Hannes Moser (nothing,
would not pay), Joanna Wiśniewska (10% at resort hotels in high season). The value boxes are percents of the calls, in
the founder's unit and period; the price picks are two codes, the pilot's rung and the licence's rung, each placed
against the founder's €3,000 and €1,000.

## Status today

Same idea (SITE, 2026-10-22): "Turn missed hotel calls into paid bookings.", widened to payments, invoices and
handovers; "Running at 15+ hotel groups" (the launch said 7); "€10k+ bookings written directly into the PMS". **No
public price today** (SITE and /faq show none); the €3,000 pilot terms remain the only priced source.

## Open (what could not be sourced, and the workarounds)

- **The licence amount** was never public. €1,000 to €1,500 per hotel a month is the operator's reading of the pilot's
  monthly rate (above). Treat the plan step's reading as a reading of that derivation.
- **Dollars or euros.** YC-L says "$5,000", YC-C "€5,000" for the same hotel; the pilot fee is in euros and the company
  is in Munich, so the entry is in euros. The market is DE, and the golden corpus's rule U (US only) is a note.
- **The "> 8 hotels" / "10 hotels" roll-out threshold** in TERMS and YC-L disagree; the entry does not use it.
- **Job titles.** Neither the agent nor the director is named in public; both are my choices (items 1 and 3).
- **The 5% is the founders' claim** for "the best" offices; no independent figure was sought.
- **UPFRONT_THEN has no "credited" or "money-back" flag**; the fee is a plain up-front amount (header).

insights.line: What would make it worth more?

whys.g1: Karim and Ingrid both want to see missed bookings on their own phone numbers before paying, so they belong together under a plain name, and Andreas's math that the licence costs more than the lost bookings and Hannes's flat refusal on reputation grounds are each their own point and rightly stand alone.
whys.g2: There is no junk answer on this line; even Hannes's refusal to pay at any price speaks directly to the price question.

founder.order_why: The flow runs well from context to problem to idea to who pays to how it sells, but 'Offer a pilot?' (22) comes after I already named the paid €3,000 pilot as the first real step (20–21), so it reads as an afterthought.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 3 and 4 (the same context question shown twice in a row); the pilot, set as the commitment on 20–21 and offered again on 22
founder.missing: The pilot's terms: that the €3,000 is refunded if it doesn't work and credited toward the per-hotel licence on roll-out. That is the core of my 'Zero Risk Pilot' pitch, and the flow only records it as a plain up-front fee.

COMMERCIAL_B2B.order_why: The 'One more thing' screen about what would take the time in buying sits between question 5 and question 6, which breaks the numbered flow just before the final pilot question.
COMMERCIAL_B2B.asked_twice: Screens 6 and 7: the data protection review time and 'what would take the time in buying' cover largely the same ground, and screen 5's owner sign-off feeds into it too.
COMMERCIAL_B2B.missing: How we handle calls today (own agents, the after-hours call center, voicemail), and whether Codyco connects to our CRS/PMS for live rates and availability, which decides any purchase for me.

screens.instead: Rows: A data protection review of guest calls · A check that bookings land in our PMS · The hotel owner signs off · The works council agrees to AI on calls

screens.why1: Right after I named what could slow a purchase, it is obvious why Keel now asks me to pick one of those steps and put a time on it for the revenue director to answer against.
screens.why2: Data protection review, PMS, trial at one hotel and signed contract are everyday words for a German hotel group's revenue side; only the intro's 'before it went through' is a little loose.
screens.why3: I know from my own sales calls that the data protection review of guest calls is the step that drags, and roughly how long it takes, so 4 weeks is my own estimate.
screens.why4: The PMS check and the trial at one hotel overlap, because the pilot is where we prove bookings land in OPERA or Apaleo, and the German step I would expect, works council (Betriebsrat) or owner sign-off, is missing.
screens.why5: The belief says what I typed: a data protection review of guest calls, done in about 4 weeks or not needed, with nothing of Codyco's name or my pilot terms leaking to the director.
screens.instead: Which step would take longest before your group could sign? -- A data protection review of guest calls / The owner's or works council's sign-off / A trial at one hotel first / A signed contract; then: how many weeks would it take?

screens.why1: After who pays and what could slow a purchase, asking for the first real step I want from a hotel group is the obvious next move, and it is where my paid pilot belongs.
screens.why2: "First real step" and the hint's "time, data, money or a signature" are plain to me, and I answered it straight off in my own sales words.
screens.why3: The step I want from a hotel group is my own sales motion, the money-back pilot from my partnership terms, so I answer it from what I do every day.
screens.why4: The only option is the escape chip "Leave this out of the study", which fits a founder who has no paid step to test, and the free box takes my own words.
screens.why5: Keel kept the pilot at one hotel with the money back, but it wrote "3,000" without my euro sign, so a stranger does not know the currency or whether it is a fee or a monthly price.
screens.instead: Keep the question; have the belief read: In most cases the hotel group revenue director would pay €3,000 up front for a money-back pilot at one hotel now.

screens.why1: Right after I named the first step I wanted, I check the words strangers will hear, so this is exactly where it belongs.
screens.why2: A revenue director at a German hotel group reads 'a money-back pilot at one hotel' on first pass; it is how we talk about it.
screens.why3: Whether to pay for a pilot at one property is a call a revenue director makes from their own budget and experience.
screens.why4: The bar's 'probably not or no' sits on a usual five-step scale, and the one-in-three threshold is clear and fair for a paid pilot.
screens.why5: My step was '€3,000', and Keel shows a bare '3,000' with no euro sign, so the amount floats without its currency; dropping 'credited on roll-out' is acceptable under nine words.
screens.instead: In most cases the hotel group revenue director would pay €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel now.

screens.why1: Right after I named the first step (the €3,000 money-back pilot), and before the study goes out, it is obvious to ask whether strangers get offered that step at the end.
screens.why2: "Offer a pilot?" with yes or no, and a hint that shows the exact line people will see, is plain to me on first read.
screens.why3: Whether I want pilot leads from this study is my own call as founder, and pilots are exactly how I sell.
screens.why4: Yes or no covers it, the two options are distinct, and no escape chip is needed.
screens.why5: The hint's line, "Would you try this for real? Leave your email", drops the step I typed on the screens before (pay €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel), and the euro sign is already missing from the recorded step, so a yes here reads like a free trial sign-up rather than my paid pilot.
screens.instead: Offer your pilot? People who say yes see: "Codyco runs a money-back pilot at one hotel for €3,000. Want to talk about one? Leave your email." (Yes, ask them / No pilot)

screens.why1: Picking who interviews my reservation agents belongs right here, just before the link goes out, after the study itself is settled.
screens.why2: The question is plain, and the hint tells me what I need: the voice reads aloud, the text is on screen, it costs 400 credits either way, and the link goes by SMS.
screens.why3: I can play both samples and pick the voice I'd want my agents to hear, so I'm deciding from what I actually hear.
screens.why4: Two names with five-second samples cover the choice, but my respondents are German reservation agents and nothing says whether either voice speaks German or with what accent, which is the one thing I'd pick on.
screens.why5: It keeps my 'reservation agents' and leaks nothing about Codyco or the revenue director to the people being asked.
screens.instead: Who should ask reservation agents your questions, in German? Daphne (German, ▶ 5 s) · Saskia (German, ▶ 5 s)

screens.why1: Right after choosing who asks the reservation agents, it is natural to choose how the revenue directors on the commercial link will answer.
screens.why2: The choice is plain, but the label runs together as 'Daphne Daphne asks' and 'Hear her Still recording', so I have to read it twice to separate the name, the sample and the status.
screens.why3: I know my directors are busy people on phones between properties, so I can judge whether they would read and tap or talk to a video.
screens.why4: Voice, text and letting them choose cover every way I would want, they are distinct, and the readiness notes fit each one.
screens.why5: 'Directors' keeps my revenue or reservations director, and nothing of Codyco leaks into how they answer.
screens.instead: How should revenue directors answer? AI interviewer (Daphne asks aloud on video, the question also on screen; they talk, type or tap; still recording, ready in a few minutes) / Read and tap (ready now) / Let them choose

screens.why1: After choosing how directors answer, the obvious last step is to decide who receives the links, so the screen belongs at the end of the send flow.
screens.why2: It is plain, but 'Who gets a link?' doesn't say whether it means the revenue directors from the last screen or the reservation agents, and 'the Contacts page' assumes I know a Keel page I haven't seen in this flow.
screens.why3: I know which revenue directors at our 7 hotel groups and the Munich hotels I can write to by name, so I can answer this from my own network.
screens.why4: The three routes are distinct and cover how I'd reach people: my own named contacts, a list Keel finds and one open link posted in a hoteliers' group; my pick, 'by name', is there.
screens.why5: Nothing of Codyco's product or roles leaks into the screen, and my choice to send each director their own link is kept.
screens.instead: Who gets a link to the revenue directors' interview? -- People I know by name (each their own link) / People Keel finds for me (a list, a link each) / One open link I post where directors already are (e.g. a hotelier group)

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Did not hold' sits right beside the number that decides it, 'Purchase friction: 4 of 8 expect longer than 4 weeks', and the card's 'bar: no more than 2 of 8' shows why that sinks it.
screens.why_b2: Each card shows what is counted, over how many and the bar, but I have to look twice at why Existing sacrifice is over 7 while everything else is over 8, and at what '5 needed' means on Ability to pay.
screens.why_b3: The six beliefs are the ones I checked in my own words (the 5% of calls, the €3,000 money-back pilot at one hotel, the director deciding with the owner agreeing, the data protection review), with only the € sign missing from the commitment line.
screens.why_b4: The line under the title only says who answered the money questions; nothing tells me what the data protection review result means for selling the pilot, such as having the GDPR paperwork for guest calls ready before the first call.
screens.why_b5: The 8 people stay visible and 'at the bar' is not dressed up as strong, but nothing says that 8 directors is a small sample, and a verdict that hinges on 4 of 8 reads as firmer than it is.
screens.instead: Did not hold on the data protection review: 4 of 8 directors expect it to take 4 weeks to 3 months, against your bar of 2. Go in with the guest-call data protection paperwork already done, or plan the pilot around a longer start; 6 of 8 would still pay the €3,000 pilot, but this is only 8 people.

screens.why_b1: The count is right there (4 of 7 at 5% or more, the bar is 5 of 7, 1 short), but 'People disagree' never says plainly that my 5% did not hold, so I have to work out the verdict from the bar myself.
screens.why_b2: The 0–15% axis, the unit and 7 cells read fine, but the marker at 5 and 'your bar · 5 of 7' put two different fives side by side, so I need a second look to tell the 5% line from the 5-of-7 count.
screens.why_b3: It is my 5% of calls and my 'after hours, at peak, on holidays'; 'per hotel a month' is only the period added around it.
screens.why_b4: The So line repeats '1 short of the bar' and points me to the Price card, but says nothing about what a 2–10% spread means for the pitch, such as leading with peak or resort hotels where Roberto and Joanna lose 8–10%.
screens.why_b5: n is shown, Karim's exclusion and Hannes as 0 are explained, and it calls itself 'a lean, not a call' for 7 people; 'above your range' on a single 5% is only odd wording.
screens.instead: Did not hold, narrowly: 4 of 7 directors lose 5% or more of reservation calls (bar 5 of 7); losses run 0–10%, highest at resort and peak hotels, so lead with those and don't pitch 5% as typical.

screens.why_b1: The status and its line are beside the deciding number: 4 of 8 at my €3,000 and €1,000, bar 6 of 8, 2 short, so I know it fell short.
screens.why_b2: The bands, the for and against counts and my bar at 6 of 8 read plainly, but the second strip shows 4 for and 3 against, which is 7 people when 8 answered, so I had to recount to see that Hannes is missing from the monthly chart.
screens.why_b3: The numbers are mine, but my €3,000 is a money-back pilot at one hotel, credited on roll-out, and the card turns it into a plain €3,000 'per hotel, once', which is a different offer to a director running nine hotels.
screens.why_b4: The So line only restates 4 of 8 and 2 short and sends me to the Insights tab, even though the quotes on this screen already say what to do: Ingrid and Karim want to see missed bookings on their own numbers first, and Andreas says the licence costs more than the bookings.
screens.why_b5: n is visible, the small group is called 'a lean, not a call', and nothing claims more than the eight answers carry, apart from the 7-versus-8 slip on the monthly strip, which is a counting gap rather than an overstatement.
screens.instead: Did not hold: 4 of 8 directors put my €3,000 money-back pilot and €1,000 a hotel a month at or above my price, 2 short of 6. The ones below want to see missed bookings on their own phone numbers first, so lead with a measured free test before asking for the fee.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits beside '4 of 8 named your price or more · 5 needed', but the chart shows 3 of 4 for me, which clears the 2-in-3 bar, so I have to work out that the call is blocked by the 4 people who named my price and not by how they answered.
screens.why_b2: What is counted (where the money comes from) and the bar at 3 of 4 are plain, but the strip draws 5 cells (3 for, 1 against, 1 ghost) while the count line says 4 counted, so I look twice to see over how many people it is drawn.
screens.why_b3: The €3,000 up front and €1,000 per hotel a month are my numbers, but 'could find the money for it' is Keel's wording, since I only checked the decision-maker, the data protection review and the pilot commitment on the way in.
screens.why_b4: 'Ability to pay waits until 5 have' says to wait but not what to do, such as getting more directors to answer at my price or noting that 3 of the 4 who named it already have a budget line for it.
screens.why_b5: n is visible throughout, the small group is called 'a lean, not a call', and the 3 of 4 is not called a held belief.
screens.instead: 3 of the 4 directors who named €3,000 and €1,000 or more would pay from a budget line they already have, which clears your bar, but only 4 of 8 named your price and 5 are needed to call it, so get more directors to answer at your price before trusting this lean.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right beside "6 of 8 as you said or easier · bar 6 of 8 · at the bar", so I see the verdict and the number that decides it together.
screens.why_b2: Each answer has its own count, the strip shows 6 for and 2 against over 8, and the marker sits at 6, all plain on first look; the rule line explains why "could sign alone" counts for me.
screens.why_b3: The title and the belief line are exactly what I checked on the way in: the revenue director decides and the hotel's owner has to agree.
screens.why_b4: "Plan for the hotel's owner in most deals; 2 of 8 could sign alone" tells me to build the owner into my sales path, and the quote about the managing director signing after a one-hotel run backs the pilot as the way to win that owner.
screens.why_b5: The count line says this is "a lean, not a call" and n stays visible, but "in most deals" overstates 4 of 8 owner answers, which is half, and the belief only just clears its bar.
screens.instead: Holding up, only just: 6 of 8 at a bar of 6, with half needing the owner and 2 able to sign alone; bring the owner a one-hotel pilot result.

screens.why_b1: "Did not hold" sits right beside "4 of 8 expect longer than 4 weeks · bar: no more than 2 of 8", so I see the verdict and the number that decides it together.
screens.why_b2: The duration bands and the 8 people are plain, but the verdict sets the bar as no more than 2 of 8 against while the strip marks it as 6 of 8 for, so I had to work out that these are the same bar.
screens.why_b3: The title and belief line are exactly what I checked, though the bar line "You said a data protection review of guest calls." is a stray fragment.
screens.why_b4: "Plan for a cycle of 4 weeks to 3 months" gives me a timeline, but nothing about how to shorten it, for example by bringing a ready DPA and a GDPR pack into the pilot, and the reasons are pushed off to another tab.
screens.why_b5: n=8 is visible and the screen says it is a lean, not a call, but a flat "Did not hold" is firm for 8 people, and the 4 weeks to 3 months band starts exactly at my "about 4 weeks", so some of those 4 against may be at my number.
screens.instead: Leaning against, 8 people: 4 of 8 expect the data protection review to take 4 weeks to 3 months, and my bar allowed 2; none expect longer than 3 months. Put the DPA and data-protection documents into the pilot offer so the review starts on day one.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right beside 6 of 8 said yes against a bar of 6 of 8, at the bar, so I know the result and the number behind it.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts the answers to the pilot question, 6 yes, 1 probably not and 1 no, over 8 people, with my bar marked at 6, and all three are plain on first look.
screens.why_b3: Commitment and the line about paying 3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel are what I checked on the way in, though the euro sign is missing from my own figure.
screens.why_b4: "Book them into it" is concrete: take the six yeses to a paid pilot contract now.
screens.why_b5: n of 8 stays visible, the small group is called a lean and not a call, and a result exactly at the bar is not dressed up as strong.
screens.instead: Write €3,000, and add: book the six into the pilot, but start the data protection review with each on day one, since 4 of 8 expect it to take longer than 4 weeks.

screens.why_b1: Purchase friction says Did not hold beside 4 of 8 against a bar of 2, and Buyer and payer is at the bar with 6 of 8, but Price is 2 short of its bar and only says 'People disagree', which leaves me to work out that my price did not hold.
screens.why_b3: All three belief lines are the ones I checked, word for word: €3,000 up front then €1,000 per hotel a month, the data protection review within about 4 weeks, and the director deciding with the owner's agreement.
screens.why_b4: Nothing on the screen says what to do; only the group name 'Proof on their own call numbers first' and Andreas's arithmetic point toward a free measured test before the €3,000 pilot, and the line that failed outright (Purchase friction) gives me no lead at all.
screens.why_b5: The counts stay visible and the 4 who never saw the friction question are named, but 'the 2 who said no' introduces one quote, and that quote (Joanna's managing director 'would agree quickly') reads more like agreement than a no.
screens.why_b6: On price I learn things I did not type: at 4% of calls, €1,000 per hotel across nine hotels costs more than the recovered bookings bring in, and Karim and Ingrid want proof on their own call data before paying anything; but the data protection review, the line that failed, has no why at all.
screens.instead: Say my price did not hold (4 of 8, 2 short), that directors below 5% missed calls want their own numbers measured free before paying, and that nobody against the 4-week review was asked why, so I still don't know what slows it.

screens.why1: As the first screen of the buying-decision link, showing me the idea before anything is asked about buying it is exactly where it belongs.
screens.why2: PMS, OPERA Cloud, Sihot, Apaleo and handing a call to the desk are everyday words in my reservations office, so I take it in on one read.
screens.why3: Calls nobody picks up after hours, at peak and on holidays are what I pay a call center to cover, so I can judge this from my own operation.
screens.why4: It is a card to read with no options, so there is nothing to score here.
screens.why5: It reads as a shown idea about forwarding missed calls and writing bookings into the PMS, and it uses no wording that feels foreign to my trade.
screens.why6: Said aloud, it is long. The belief repeats the how almost word for word instead of pointing back to it, and 'AI answering for unanswered calls' trips the ear.
screens.instead: Imagine Codyco, an AI that answers the calls your hotels miss. ... The people building it believe it would turn those missed calls into bookings.

screens.why1: Right after the idea card, asking how many of our booking calls slip away is the obvious first thing to establish about the cost of the problem.
screens.why2: "Lost" is not how I'd put it: we talk about abandoned or unanswered calls, and "lost" could also mean calls answered but not converted into a booking, so I'd have to stop and guess which one is meant.
screens.why3: I track our abandonment rate on the reservations office reports and could tell you it was about 6 percent without looking.
screens.why4: A percent box is the right shape, but showing "None" beside "I can't recall" makes two chips where one escape is meant, and "None" only repeats typing 0.
screens.why5: The founder's window was the last 7 days and the job was calls that never got answered, and here it has drifted to last month and the vaguer "lost".
screens.why6: The question itself says well, but "a percent of the reservation calls last month, or a low and a high; none is 0" is a mouthful of instructions you have to unpick by ear.
screens.instead: Last month, about what share of the booking calls to your reservations office went unanswered? Say a percent. Or say you can't recall.

screens.why1: Right after I have said what share of calls we lose, asking what it would be worth to me to catch them is the obvious next step for someone who signs off on these tools.
screens.why2: Up front, a month and per hotel are exactly how vendors quote reservation tools to me, so I can answer on first reading.
screens.why3: Pricing booking and reservation tools per property is my job, so I can answer from what we have paid for similar services.
screens.why4: The monthly ladder starts too high, so where I would really land (a few hundred euros a hotel) all falls into Under €500; and there is no way to say I would rather pay per booking or as a share of revenue, which is how I think about the 6% I pay today.
screens.why5: Only the name and line from the idea card reach me, and per hotel, up front and monthly are the founder's own terms, kept.
screens.why6: Each step holds as a list, but it is two price questions in two steps each, the to-under bands are a mouthful when heard, and 'Or say you can't say' sounds clumsy aloud.
screens.instead: What would Codyco be worth to you a month, per hotel? Under €200; €200 to under €500; €500 to under €1,000; €1,000 or more; or I'd only pay per booking it brings in. Or say I can't say.

screens.why1: Right after I named a price, asking where the money would come from is the obvious next step for whoever holds the budget.
screens.why2: Budget line, signed off and other spending are words I use every week with our finance people, so I can answer on first reading.
screens.why3: As the revenue director I know which budget a reservations tool would sit in, and whether I would need new money or would move it from the call center contract.
screens.why4: The first four cover it, but 'There was no budget for it' is in the past tense on a would-question and reads like 'we would not buy', not like a source of money.
screens.why5: It only points back to my own price and names nothing of the founder's product or roles beyond what the idea card already showed me.
screens.why6: The four options say well as a list, but 'Or say you can't say' is clumsy to hear, and the past-tense last option jars when spoken after a would-question.
screens.instead: If you went ahead at that price, where would the money come from? A budget line we already have; a new budget line someone signs off; moved from other spending, such as the call center; or we would not find the money. Or: I can't say.

screens.why1: Right after I said what Codyco is worth and where the money would come from, it's obvious to ask whether I can sign that off myself.
screens.why2: 'Sign off' and an approval limit in euros are everyday words for me as a revenue director, and I'd answer on first hearing.
screens.why3: I know my own approval limit and who has to countersign above it, so I can answer from fact, not a guess.
screens.why4: At a hotel group the person above me is usually our managing director or CFO rather than 'the hotel's owner', so that option fits me poorly; 'someone else's decision' and 'several people' also partly cover the same case.
screens.why5: It keeps only the €3,000 up-front figure and drops the €1,000 to €2,500 a month I just gave, and it frames the decision per hotel and per owner when I buy for the group.
screens.why6: The stem and the four parallel options say well, but the closing 'Or say you can't say' sounds clumsy when heard.
screens.instead: Could you sign off on about €3,000 per hotel plus the monthly fee yourself, or would someone else have to agree? — Yes, I could sign off myself · No, our managing director or CFO would · No, the property owners would · No, several people would have to agree · I can't say

screens.why1: Right after asking whether I could sign off myself, it makes sense to ask what else has to clear before a tool that handles guest calls can go live, and in Germany that means data protection.
screens.why2: A data protection review of guest calls is exactly how we would describe going through our Datenschutzbeauftragter before anything touches recorded calls, so I can answer on first reading.
screens.why3: I've pushed call recording and reservation tools through our data protection officer before, so I know roughly how long it takes for us.
screens.why4: The bands don't overlap, they cover everything from a quick check to the half-year it can take when the works council gets involved, 'It wouldn't be needed' is a real option, and 'I can't tell' is the right escape.
screens.why5: It names the product shown on the idea card and a real step in buying it, with no internal terms or roles leaking through.
screens.why6: It is one short question, the first step is four options I can hold, and the follow-up pair is easy to hear, so I could answer after hearing it once.

screens.why1: Right after I said how long a data protection review of guest calls would take, asking what would actually eat that time is the natural next step.
screens.why2: Short and plain; I'd answer straight away with the data protection officer, the works council and the owners' sign-off.
screens.why3: I run these purchases for our group, so I know what holds them up: the DSGVO review of recorded guest calls, the Betriebsrat, and IT hooking it into our PMS and phone system.
screens.why4: A box to type in, no options.
screens.why5: It asks about buying in general rather than the data protection review I was just asked about, so it drifts a little from the step the founder named, though nothing leaks.
screens.why6: One short question, nine words, easy to hear once and answer.
screens.instead: What would take the time in getting Codyco through data protection and sign-off?

screens.why1: After the price, the budget, the sign-off and the data protection review, asking whether I would actually put money on a pilot is the obvious last question.
screens.why2: "Money-back pilot at one hotel" is how I'd talk, but "3,000" has no euro sign or word, so I have to work out from the earlier screens that it means €3,000 and not 3,000 a month or per call.
screens.why3: Whether I'd fund a pilot at one of our hotels is exactly the kind of call I make myself, and I said earlier that €3,000 per hotel is within what I can sign off.
screens.why4: The scale is lopsided: it has a firm yes, a "probably not" and a no, but no "probably yes" or "yes, if the data protection review clears", which is where I'd really land.
screens.why5: "AI answering for unanswered calls" and a pilot at one hotel keep the idea, but dropping the euro from the €3,000 already given lets the amount drift.
screens.why6: Said aloud, "3,000" with no currency doesn't say well, and the first option repeats the whole stem before the short "probably not" and "no", so the list is uneven to hold.
screens.instead: If it were ready today, would you pay €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel, or not? Yes · Probably yes · Probably not · No
